toc.title: Tip one: create a safer environment
Tip two: use your anxiety with fidgets
Tip three: use your anxiety with movement
Tip five: validate, normalize, give permission

blocks.p: Anxiety is probably something you're intimately familiar with. But do you know what anxiety actually is, and what to do about it? Here are five super practical, free tips to help reduce your anxiety in your day-to-day life.

You're probably aware of anxiety on an experiential level. You consciously know when you feel it. But depending on who you ask, anxiety could be a number of things. You may have heard that it's a chemical imbalance, or a character defect, like you're not strong enough. Or that it's a hereditary condition, or a survival response, or maybe even the influence of the devil.
From the point of view of the neuroscience of the Polyvagal Theory, anxiety is something very specific, and I think much more easily understandable:
Anxiety is the emotional experience of being stuck in a polyvagal state of flight.

If you're not safe, if you can't connect with yourself and connect with others, your body shifts into a defensive state. The first state it shifts to is flight. It prepares to mobilize, to get out of that situation and get to safety.

But if you can't act on that impulse to get away, the body just remains in the flight state. Day to day, that's experienced as anxiety, nervousness, worry, anticipation, rumination. When you're feeling anxious, don't you kind of want to leave whatever situation you're in? You probably want to get away, to make space, to get to safety, and I'd assume somewhere more predictable and less stimulating.

The goal here is not to make anxiety go away. Honestly, that's not my goal, though it might be the natural result of these tips. It's more about using your body's natural potential for being in its safety state, and using the activation of your flight state: the mobility that's already in your system.
And these things need to be practical. They need to be things you can use in your day-to-day life, quickly and easily, without drawing a lot of attention to yourself or spending money.

Before the five tips, a bonus. You have to have the bare bones basics in place: a good enough diet, enough movement in your life, enough sleep. I'm not going to tell you what the right amount of each is. I think it's different from person to person, so I'm going to trust you on this. And socialize, as best you can, with people who are safe in your life.

I really think you need those in place before moving on. If you don't have them, do as well as you possibly can, then do the other tips, and maybe come back to the basics. You might be able to handle them differently then.

I also think some structure and predictability in your life is a very good idea. Being able to predict what's coming next is a cue of safety. It actually helps to reduce anxiety, worrying, and wondering.

blocks.h: Tip one: create a safer environment

blocks.p: The environment you're in right now, the one at work, at home, at a friend's house, the restaurants you go to: all of these affect your neuroception of safety or danger.

Your senses bring in cues from the external environment: what you see, hear, smell, taste, and touch. Those cues go to your brainstem, which detects whether it's safe or dangerous and shifts your body into a state of safety or defense. So if you create an environment that provides more safety cues, you increase the chances of being in your safety state, and of reducing your anxiety.

I don't need you to completely overhaul your space. I don't need you to paint the walls or go buy new furniture. If you can afford it, great, but not all of us can. Instead, identify one piece of your environment you do have control over. If you're renting an apartment with somebody, maybe it's your room. If your house is a disaster and everywhere is overwhelming, maybe you can't even pick one room. Maybe it's just a corner of a room. One place you can take control of and begin to increase the safety cues.
There are probably things you can do right now with the environment you're in (as long as you're not driving):

ul: Clear up any clutter, crumbs, or garbage. Throw away what needs to go in the garbage or the recycling.
Adjust the lighting if you can. Use a dimmer, or open the blinds and let some daylight in.
Organize and tidy up. If there are knickknacks around you that don't give you a sense of calm and are just more visual clutter, get rid of them or move them.
Bring in things that feel more good for you, maybe from a different part of your home or workplace, into that little safety environment.

blocks.p: The point is not to feel happy. If you feel happy, great. The point is to create a space that lets you breathe a bit easier, and reduces or manages the anxiety you might otherwise have.

blocks.h: Tip two: use your anxiety with fidgets

blocks.p: If you have anxiety, that indicates you're in a flight state, which means you have the impulse to move. So wouldn't it make sense to use your body's potential for movement?

I'm not saying get up and run. You can, if you like and if you're able, but I think a less embarrassing and maybe more doable way to use some of your anxious flight energy is through fidgets. I like to experiment with different ones. Pick one or two that really spark something within you, where there's more of a sense of like versus dislike.

It doesn't have to bring you happiness. It just needs to bring a sensation or feeling of relief. Maybe soothing, maybe calm. When you find the right fidget, there's this feeling of, "Ooh, I like that." That's what we're looking for.

It has to be something you can use mindfully, and maybe discreetly depending on where you are. If you're at a potluck at work, or at your desk, and you don't want to make a scene with your fidget, you might just keep it in your pocket: something you can squeeze or roll around in your fingers. Fidgeting with curiosity and mindfulness, really experiencing what it feels like, can help reduce the anxious feelings of your flight state. The mindfulness is a really big piece of this.

blocks.h: Tip three: use your anxiety with movement

blocks.p: Maybe fidgets aren't enough, and you'd benefit from getting up and moving around. That's where a bigger type of movement comes in handy. Maybe you're not sprinting. Maybe you're taking a walk, but doing it mindfully.

I like to take a walk around the block when I'm at work. When I do, I typically don't bring my earbuds or my phone. I do it quietly and really take in my external environment. I listen to what's around me, the birds and whatnot.

If you don't want to get up and walk around, flexing and releasing your muscles mindfully can be really helpful. If you're at your desk or your dinner table and you're feeling anxious, tense your calves and then release them, or tense your thighs and release them. Really squeeze, and then when you're ready, let it go and relax.

You can also run or bike, if you're able. Those can be great ways to mindfully use the flight energy in your system. But you can't just get up and run. You have to actually notice and experience what it's like for your muscles to move. On that walk, notice what it's like for your feet to push off the pavement, your calves and thighs to flex, your knees to bend. Really experience those little micro movements, and take in the external environment as well. Do one thing at a time. You can shift back and forth between what your body is doing and what the world around you is like. Think of these as mini moments to focus on.

There are so many breath recommendations out there. I don't personally like to give a specific breathing regimen or prescription. To me, your body knows how to breathe, based on whatever state it's in.

So rather than trying to change that, what if we just let your body breathe the way it needs to? And yes, you guessed it: what if we did it mindfully? When you mindfully feel into and notice your breathing, it gives your body permission to breathe the way it already knows how to. You don't have to change anything. You just allow it and mindfully experience it. If you can do that, the process of self-regulation can open up, and climbing the polyvagal ladder can happen.
If you want something more directive, the only controlled breathing I like to recommend is belly breathing with an extended exhale:

ol: Take a breath mindfully into your belly if you can. I recommend through the nose, and you should really feel your belly expand. I don't think that's completely necessary, but it's what I recommend.
Pause ever so briefly, if it's comfortable. Again, not necessary.

Breathe out through your mouth, like you're blowing out a birthday candle, but slowly. Make the exhale slower than the inhale, as long as it's comfortable. I don't need you to count four or five seconds. Just extend it a little longer than you normally would.

blocks.p: What I like to tell myself is something I got from Peter Levine, though I don't remember the source: trust that the next breath will come. It's that mindfulness, and that trust that your body knows what it needs. You're simply aligning with your capacity for self-regulation and letting it happen.

It's totally okay to let your body breathe the way it wants to, and it might want to breathe into your chest. It can be really hard to breathe into your belly when you're anxious. If you have to breathe into your chest, that's fine. Do it mindfully, and extend the exhale. That's really the most important piece. When you breathe out, the parasympathetic safety state pathways come on. Extending the exhale lets them stay active a little longer. Let yourself settle into that exhale as best you can, and allow your body to relax.
Jill Miller put the same idea simply when she was on the podcast:

q: A sedating breath... is a breath where the exhale is longer than the inhale.
blocks.cite: Jill Miller, [Jill Miller: Yoga & the Polyvagal Theory part 1 (episode 33)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/161d5c18-d051-477f-b07b-bd7fb88306d6)

blocks.p: You can do this anywhere. It's pretty darn discreet. At work or at home, take that mindful breath into your belly and let it out slowly. It's not going to make a big scene.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Tip five: validate, normalize, give permission

blocks.p: This tip has three parts. It's top-down anxiety management. I think it's good for any of the polyvagal defensive states, but here we're focusing on anxiety from the flight state.

Using top-down cognitions to change or soften a defensive state can be very challenging. So if you go this route, don't do it when you're too far into the anxiety. Try to catch it early: a little anxiety, nervousness, worry. If you're in a full-on panic attack, I don't know how helpful this is, unless you've really practiced it and have a pretty good amount of distress tolerance. Use it when it's actually usable.

Validating just means acknowledging that the anxiety you're experiencing is real. It's happening. It's not judging it, dismissing it, minimizing it, or even being okay with it. It's just saying: it's real. I am feeling anxiety. If a friend told you they were going through anxiety, you'd probably say something like, "Yeah, it sounds like you feel really anxious." It's the same thing, without judging it.
Normalizing means making sense of your anxiety based on the context you're in, or the context of your larger life. It answers the question: does my anxiety make sense?

Maybe you saw somebody from your past you really did not want to be around again. You'll probably feel anxious, because the flight state is on and you may need to leave. So you can normalize it: yes, it makes sense for me to feel anxious here. I have every reason to want to leave. That feeling makes sense, and it could even be acted on.

Or maybe you hear a voice that reminds you of that person, or a certain phrase that triggers that anxiousness. The person isn't there. You're not actually in danger. But does the anxiety make sense based on the larger context of your life? I would say yes. So you can normalize it that way too. You could also ask yourself: if anybody else had my life and was in this situation and felt anxiety, would that make sense? If the answer is yes, that's also normalization.
After you've validated and normalized, the third part is giving your anxiety permission to be there.

I'm not saying dwell on it. I'm not saying get sucked into the vortex of anxiety and the flight state, or ruminate until it turns into a chaotic panic attack. Remember, this top-down tip is for when the anxiety is manageable, not when it's out of control.

The anxiety isn't going anywhere. It's already there. It may exist within you a lot, maybe day in and day out. So it's recognizing that it's there, it makes sense, and, if you want to personify it: "Okay, you're welcome to be here within me. I can't fight this. You exist within me anyway. So you may stay here with me while I do something that helps me anchor my safety state."

You can even give it a visualization. I like to picture putting it in my pocket: "Hey, anxiety, I see you. I can't force you to go away, so I'm going to stick you in my pocket and let you hang out with me while I fidget with something, or smell a scent I like, or go to the safety environment in my home, or go for a walk and take in some sunshine."
Each of these is helpful on its own. If you just want to pick one, do the one you feel the most hope and potential in. But you can also bring them together, and I think they add on to each other:

ol: Before anything else, create that space in your life that gives you passive cues of safety, ready to turn to when you need it. And practice being in safety as well.
When you notice a tolerable level of anxiety, not too much, validate it, normalize it, and give it permission to be there with you. Stick it in your pocket.
Go to your safety environment if you need to, reduce the environmental overwhelm, and start to receive those passive safety cues.
Mindfully use a fidget, some movement, or your breathing, and allow the anxious feeling to be present as you also anchor yourself in your safety state.

blocks.p: And as a bonus, if you're able to, the next step is to be a witness to the internal sensations, images, emotions, and cognitions. It helps to build language for these things so you can recognize them and name them. I think once you can name things, they become more manageable as well.
